rv.q: There are plenty of places in which the updating gives us something new and precious, something fresh to consider about this old, frightening story.
It's no exaggeration to say that this production of Long Day's Journey Into Night is a stroke of genius, and it really must be seen to appreciate how startlingly well it works.
This experiment works for both Mr. O'Neill and Mr. O'Hara, giving us a new, pocket-sized way to look at 'Long Day's Journey.'
It's a brave and complicated look at how the occluded world that O'Neill investigated decades ago remains just as shrouded in secrecy, even when it becomes impossible to ignore.
The links forged in this Audible Theater production at times go slack.
Saving O'Hara's shorter performance journey from slipping over the line into utter travesty is his direction, for the most part, of the estimable actors.
Having now seen the production, I can only say that I'm still looking forward to someday seeing Bill Camp and Elizabeth Marvel in Long Day's Journey into Night .
Jessica Lange has here written the dictionary on various forms of nuanced, nervous laughter, fluttering hands, darting eyes, and erratic vocal change.
However, the play still felt long. It became especially tedious especially in the last half hour of the play.

cn.t: O'Hara's heavily cut, COVID-era update of O'Neill's masterpiece divides critics. Strong performances from Camp and Marvel can't overcome a controversial modern setting that many find unnecessary, though some praise the intriguing reimagining.
